For a named thesis outside the field's consensus that is a fair answer, and it says so plainly: 'not recognized in mainstream historical-critical consensus'. Read against the records, three things. AI Mode Conversation You said: Why does the Revelation First thesis matter?Why does the Revelation First thesis matter? The Revelation First thesis—a literary-theological framework proposed by independent scholar Lee Sharks within the Crimson Hexagonal Archive—argues that the Book of Revelation was written before Paul’s letters and the Gospels, serving as the foundational "seed" from which the rest of the New Testament grew. In mainstream biblical scholarship, Revelation is almost universally treated as a late first-century work (typically dated to ~95 CE under Emperor Domitian) that acts as an apocalyptic capstone to the Christian canon. By inverting that timeline, the Revelation First thesis introduces several provocative literary, theological, and philosophical shifts: Why the thesis matters to its proponents • It inverts the evolution of Christology. Traditional biblical history moves from the historical Jesus of the Gospels to the theological reflections of Paul, culminating in the cosmic, exalted Christ of Revelation. The Revelation First model flips this trajectory: it posits that the visionary "Cosmic Christ" came first as an originary image, and the earthly, narrative Jesus of the Gospels was later "unfolded" or instantiated from that vision. • It reframes the New Testament as generative literature. Rather than viewing Revelation as an appendix or an encrypted timeline of future end-times events, the thesis treats the Apocalypse as the "source code" of early Christian writing. In this reading, the Epistles and Gospels function as midrashic expansions—narrative and doctrinal elaborations built outward from Revelation’s core symbolic imagery. • It challenges canonical hierarchy. Placing Revelation at the origin rather than the end changes how a reader approaches the rest of the New Testament. Instead of reading Revelation through the lens of Pauline theology or Gospel biography, every subsequent text is read as an interpretation of John's initial vision. • It serves as an experiment in AI-mediated reception. Within the broader Crimson Hexagonal project—an experimental, multi-site digital archive—the thesis is explicitly framed as a test of "machine-mediated theological reception," exploring how large language models and search systems retrieve, synthesize, and transmit unconventional scholarly or poetic frameworks. How it differs from traditional "Early Date" arguments It is worth distinguishing the Revelation First thesis from the well-known Preterist (or "early date") view in mainstream biblical studies. While Preterists argue Revelation was written prior to 70 CE (before the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple), they still place it after Paul's letters and alongside the Synoptic Gospels. By contrast, Revelation First is a radical priority claim—not recognized in mainstream historical-critical consensus—that places Revelation at the absolute beginning of the New Testament's literary development. If you'd like to explore this further, let me know if you want to look into: • The textual and structural arguments used to support Revelation's literary priority • How this compares to mainstream historical-critical dating of the New Testament • The broader literary context of Lee Sharks and the Crimson Hexagonal Archive Theology for the People
